title: Overview and justification
body:
This short course is about academic writing: not a single talent some people have and others do not, but a process you can learn to work through. By the end you will be able to describe writing as a series of stages, plan a piece and get a first draft down, and improve that draft by getting the basics of structure and clarity right.

This matters because writing is how most of your work is assessed, in every subject. Students who treat writing as one anxious sitting that has to come out right first time make it far harder than it needs to be. Knowing the process, and having a few reliable habits, changes how you start, how you revise, and the marks your work earns.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this course, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe academic writing as a process of distinct stages
plan a piece of writing and get a first draft down
improve a draft by getting the basics of structure and clarity right.

title: In real academic practice
body: Academic writing is the main way your learning is judged. Every essay, report and reflective piece you are set draws on the same underlying process: understand the task, plan, draft, and revise. Build the habit now and it carries into every module of your degree, and into the clear, organised writing that professional work later asks of you.

title: Signpost
body: The course has three short lessons. First, writing as a process: why a good piece of work is made in stages, not in one sitting. Second, understanding the task and getting a draft down: reading the question, planning, and getting started. Third, getting the basics right: editing a draft for structure and clarity. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: Many students think of writing as something you either can or cannot do, and sit down hoping the finished essay will come out in one go. It rarely does, and treating it that way makes writing harder and more stressful than it needs to be. Academic writing is better understood as a process: a series of stages you move through, each with its own job. This lesson looks at what that process is, so that writing stops being a single daunting act and becomes a set of steps you can follow.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are early in your studies, and you have probably written essays at school. At this stage you are not expected to produce polished, argument-driven writing straight away. The aim is to understand writing as a process and recognise its stages, so you have a dependable way to approach any piece of writing you are set.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: describe academic writing as a process made of distinct stages, not a single act
recognise the writing process in a worked example of two students' approaches
identify why getting a draft down matters when you start writing in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Academic writing is not a single burst of inspiration; it is a process made of distinct stages. You understand the task, plan what you want to say, get a first draft down, and then revise it into something good. The stages are not all done at once, and the first version is never meant to be the last.

This matters because the most common mistake is to collapse the whole process into one sitting, trying to produce finished sentences from a blank page. A general principle is worth holding on to: it is better to have a rough draft to work with than nothing at all. The draft is raw material you improve, not a performance you have to get right first time.

title: Reflective prompt
body: When you last had a piece of writing to do, did you try to get it perfect from the first line, or work in stages? What is one thing you could do differently to treat your next piece as a process?

title: Summary
body: Academic writing is a process, not a single act of getting it right first time: you understand the task, plan, draft, and then revise. You can now describe those stages and recognise the process in how a student approaches a piece of writing. Holding on to one principle, that it is better to have a rough draft to work with than nothing at all, takes the pressure off the blank page. The next lesson turns the process into practice: understanding the task, planning, and getting a first draft down.

title: Orientation
body: In the last lesson you saw that writing is a process. This lesson is about how it starts. Before you can plan or draft, you need to understand what the task is actually asking; then a short plan turns that understanding into a shape; then you get a first draft down. The hardest part, the blank page, is easier once you know what to do first.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to produce a perfect plan or a polished draft. The aim here is to read a question for what it is really asking, sketch a rough plan, and get words on the page without waiting for them to be right.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: identify the steer and the keywords in an assignment task
give an example of turning a plan into a first draft
choose a sensible first move when faced with a blank page in {{context}}.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Every assignment task has two things worth reading closely: its steer and its keywords. The steer is the instruction word, such as analyse, discuss, compare or evaluate, that tells you the approach to take. The keywords are the specific terms that fix the topic and its limits. Reading both carefully is the first stage of writing, because it decides what everything else has to do.

Planning comes next: it is the bridge between the reading you have done and the writing you are about to do, a rough map of your main points and their order. With a plan in place, the first draft has a job that is finally manageable, not to be perfect, but simply to get the plan into sentences on the page, where you can then improve it.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the last assignment you were set. Did you read it closely for its steer and keywords, or start writing straight away? What could you have planned before you began?

title: Summary
body: Writing starts with understanding the task: its steer, which tells you how to answer, and its keywords, which fix what to answer. A rough plan then bridges your reading and your writing, and a first draft turns that plan into sentences you can improve. You can now read a task for its steer and keywords, turn a plan into a draft, and make a sensible first move at the blank page. The next lesson is about improving that draft: getting the basics right.

title: Orientation
body: You have a first draft. This lesson is about what to do with it. A draft is raw material, and the stage that turns it into good writing is revision: editing it to improve structure and clarity, then proofreading to catch the small errors. Knowing a few basics here is what separates a rushed piece from one that reads well.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: You are not expected to edit like a professional yet. The aim is to tell editing apart from proofreading, know a few reliable moves for making a draft clearer, and recognise the common errors that are easy to fix once you look for them.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: use the basics of clear writing (structure, clarity and correcting common errors) to improve a draft
tell editing apart from proofreading
match a revision move in {{context}} to the problem it fixes.

title: Concept: definition
body:
Revising a draft has two different jobs, and it helps to keep them apart. Editing is the bigger job: reordering points, cutting or adding text, sharpening how things are expressed, and making paragraphs do their work. Proofreading is the final polish: catching typos, slips and small errors once the writing itself is settled.

Two basics carry most of the weight. Structure means arranging points so a reader can follow them, with each paragraph making one clear point and connecting to the ones around it. Clarity means writing sentences a reader understands first time, often as simply as putting them in subject-verb-object order, so it is clear who did what. Get these right and the writing works, whatever the subject.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Look back at a piece of writing you handed in. Did you edit it for structure and clarity, or only proofread for typos? What is one editing move you could make next time?

title: Summary
body: Revising a draft has two jobs: editing, which improves structure and clarity by reordering, cutting, adding and rewriting, and proofreading, which polishes the surface at the end. Two basics do most of the work: a clear structure a reader can follow, and clear subject-verb-object sentences. You can now improve a draft, tell editing apart from proofreading, and match a revision move to the problem it fixes. With the process, a way to start, and the basics of revision in place, you are ready to write.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Academic writing is no longer a single daunting act: it is a process you can work through. You can describe its stages, that is, understanding the task, planning, drafting and revising. You can read a task for its steer and keywords, plan, and get a first draft down rather than waiting for perfect sentences. And you can improve that draft by getting the basics right: a clear structure and clear sentences, editing before you proofread. Look back at the confidence check: comparing where you started with where you are now shows how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: From here, this process is something you use in every module. Each essay you plan before you write, each rough draft you get down and then improve, each piece you edit for structure before proofreading, is the same process at work. It is also what professional life rewards: clear, organised writing produced to a deadline travels well beyond your degree.

title: Where this goes next
body: Two directions build on this. Going deeper: the intermediate and advanced academic writing courses take the process into building an argument, using sources, and writing within your own discipline. Going wider: the same habits underpin Criticality, Referencing and Researching, where you put clear writing to work on real tasks.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: What writing as a process looks like
body: Four everyday ideas about academic writing. Turn each card to see past the common misunderstanding.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over. Work through all four.

back.body: A good piece of writing is not produced in one go from start to finish. It is built in stages - understanding, planning, drafting, revising - each done at a different time, with the draft improving as you go.

front.title: Not a talent you are born with

back.body: Writing well is not a gift some students have and others lack. It is the result of a process anyone can follow. The students whose work reads well are usually the ones who planned and revised, not the ones who wrote fastest.

front.title: The first draft is meant to be rough

back.body: The job of a first draft is simply to exist. It is better to have something imperfect on the page to work with than a blank screen you are waiting to fill with perfect sentences.

front.title: Planning is the most important stage

back.body: The stage that makes the biggest difference is planning: deciding what you want to say, and in what order, before you try to say it well. Time spent planning saves far more time later.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Consider two students given the same essay to write.

{{learner-a}} opens a blank document and tries to write the finished essay from the first sentence onwards, polishing each line before moving on. Hours pass, little is written, and what is there cannot be changed without starting again. {{learner-a}} is treating writing as a single performance that must be perfect first time. This is the harder way.

{{learner-b}} starts by noting what the question is really asking, jots a rough plan of the main points, then writes a quick first draft without worrying about how it sounds. With a whole draft to work with, {{learner-b}} goes back and improves it: reordering points, sharpening sentences, fixing errors. {{learner-b}} is treating writing as a process. This is the easier way, and the better essay.

Both students spent the same time. Only {{learner-b}} used it as a process, turning a blank page into a draft and a draft into a finished piece.

title: Working as a process
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These habits turn writing into a process you can follow. Try them on your next piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I worked out what the question is actually asking before I start writing?
Have I made a rough plan of my main points and their order?
Have I got a first draft down without stopping to perfect each sentence?
Have I treated that first draft as raw material to improve, not a finished piece?
Have I left time to revise, rather than finishing at the first draft?
Have I noticed when I am trying to write and edit at the same time?

_items.text: A single talent that some students have and others do not.
_items.feedback: Writing well is a process anyone can follow, not an inborn talent.

_items.text: One careful sitting in which the finished essay is produced from start to finish.
_items.feedback: Trying to produce the finished piece in one sitting is the mistake this lesson warns against.

_items.text: A matter of writing as many words as quickly as possible.
_items.feedback: Quantity and speed are not what make writing good.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic writing is a process of distinct stages, not a talent, a single sitting or a word count.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the option about distinct stages you work through.
_incorrect.final: Academic writing is a process of understanding, planning, drafting and revising. The other options mistake it for a talent, a single sitting, or a word count.

title: Formative check: recognising the process
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's approach more effective?

ariaQuestion: What made the second student's approach more effective?

_items.text: They typed faster than the first student.
_items.feedback: Speed is not what made the difference.

_items.text: They worked in stages - planning, drafting, then revising - rather than trying to write it perfectly first time.
_items.feedback: Yes. Working in stages is what made the approach effective.

_items.text: They waited until they could write perfect sentences before starting.
_items.feedback: That is the first student's harder approach, not the second's.

_items.text: They wrote the whole essay in a single sitting.
_items.feedback: The second student worked in stages, not in one sitting.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student planned, drafted and then revised, rather than trying to be perfect first time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for what the second student DID differently, that is, working in stages.
_incorrect.final: The second student was more effective because they worked in stages. Speed, waiting for perfect sentences, or one long sitting are not it.

title: Formative check: why a draft matters
displayTitle: You are about to start a piece of writing in {{context}}. Why does getting a rough first draft down matter?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why does getting a rough first draft down matter?

_items.text: A draft gives you raw material to improve, which is better than a blank page you are waiting to fill perfectly.
_items.feedback: Yes. In {{context}}, a rough draft you can improve beats a blank page every time.

_items.text: A first draft should already be the finished, polished version.
_items.feedback: A first draft is meant to be rough, not finished.

_items.text: It lets you reach the word count before you have planned anything.
_items.feedback: Hitting a word count is not the point of a draft.

_items.text: It means you will not need to revise the writing afterwards.
_items.feedback: A draft is the start of revision, not a way to avoid it.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A rough draft in {{context}} gives you raw material to improve, which beats a blank page.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a rough draft gives you that a blank page does not.
_incorrect.final: Getting a draft down matters because it gives you raw material to improve. It is not meant to be finished, a shortcut to the word count, or a way to skip revising.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: Getting started, step by step
body: Four moves that take you from a task to a first draft. Open each to see the step.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Read the steer
_items.body: The steer is the instruction word in the task: analyse, discuss, compare, evaluate. It tells you what kind of thinking the question wants. 'Describe' and 'evaluate' ask for very different essays, so the steer shapes everything that follows.

_items.title: Find the keywords
_items.body: The keywords fix the topic and its limits: the specific terms, the time period, the place, the scope. Underlining them stops you writing a good essay on the wrong question, a common and costly mistake.

_items.title: Make a rough plan
_items.body: A plan is a short map of your main points and the order they come in. It does not need to be neat. Its job is to turn a vague sense of what you want to say into a shape you can write to.

_items.title: Get a draft down
_items.body: With a plan in front of you, write a quick first draft that follows it. Do not stop to perfect sentences. The aim is a complete rough version you can then improve, not a finished paragraph you are afraid to change.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students are set the same essay: 'Discuss the causes of a historical event.'

{{learner-a}} reads the title once, spots the topic, and starts writing everything known about the event. He makes no plan and pays no attention to the word 'discuss', so the essay becomes a long description that never weighs the causes against each other. The task's steer was missed, and a lot of effort goes into answering a question that was not asked.

{{learner-b}} reads the title closely, underlines 'discuss' and 'causes', and notes that the essay must weigh several causes rather than just list them. A quick plan sets out three causes and an order. Then {{learner-b}} writes a rough draft straight from the plan, not worrying yet about style, ready to improve it next.

Both students understood the event. Only {{learner-b}} read the task, planned, and turned that plan into a draft, the moves that make the writing answer the question.

displayTitle: How to do it
body: These moves take you from a task to a first draft. Try them on your next assignment.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I identified the steer, the instruction word that says how to answer?
Have I underlined the keywords that fix the topic and its limits?
Have I checked I am answering the question asked, not one I would prefer?
Have I made a rough plan of my main points and their order?
Have I written a first draft straight from the plan, without stopping to perfect it?
Have I resisted editing sentences before the whole draft exists?

title: Formative check: the steer
displayTitle: In an assignment task, what is the 'steer'?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the steer in an assignment task?

_items.text: The instruction word - such as analyse, discuss or evaluate - that tells you how to approach the question.
_items.feedback: Yes. The steer is the instruction word that sets the approach.

_items.text: The specific topic terms that fix what the essay is about.
_items.feedback: Those are the keywords, not the steer.

_items.text: The number of words the essay should be.
_items.feedback: The word count is not the steer.

_items.text: The reading list attached to the question.
_items.feedback: The reading list is not the steer.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The steer is the instruction word that tells you how to approach the question.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which part of a task tells you HOW to answer, rather than what about?
_incorrect.final: The steer is the instruction word, such as analyse or discuss. The topic terms are keywords; the word count and reading list are neither.

title: Formative check: plan into draft
displayTitle: In the worked example, what did the second student do to turn understanding into a draft?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What did the second student do to turn understanding into a draft?

_items.text: They wrote down everything they knew about the topic without a plan.
_items.feedback: That is the first student's approach, and it missed the steer.

_items.text: They made a rough plan from the task and wrote a first draft straight from that plan.
_items.feedback: Yes. A plan, then a draft from the plan, is the move.

_items.text: They polished the opening paragraph until it was perfect before continuing.
_items.feedback: Perfecting one paragraph is not what turned understanding into a draft.

_items.text: They waited until they fully understood the topic before writing anything.
_items.feedback: They did not wait; they planned and drafted.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student planned from the task and drafted straight from the plan.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan-then-draft move, rather than a plan-free dump or endless polishing.
_incorrect.final: The second student made a rough plan and wrote a draft from it. Writing without a plan, perfecting one paragraph, or waiting indefinitely are not it.

title: Formative check: the first move
displayTitle: You are faced with a blank page for a piece of writing in {{context}}. Which is the sensible first move this lesson recommends?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which is the sensible first move at a blank page?

_items.text: Read the task for its steer and keywords, then sketch a rough plan before drafting.
_items.feedback: Yes. Understand the task and plan before you draft in {{context}}.

_items.text: Start writing the finished opening paragraph straight away.
_items.feedback: Perfecting an opening before you understand the task is the harder way.

_items.text: Write down everything you know until you reach the word count.
_items.feedback: A word-count dump ignores the task and the plan.

_items.text: Wait until you feel inspired enough to write it perfectly.
_items.feedback: Waiting for inspiration leaves the page blank; a plan gets you moving.

_feedback.correct: That's right. In {{context}}, read the task for its steer and keywords, then plan before drafting.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What comes before drafting: understanding the task and planning.
_incorrect.final: The sensible first move is to read the task for its steer and keywords and sketch a plan. Perfecting an opening, dumping everything you know, or waiting for inspiration are not it.

title: Explore the concept
displayTitle: The basics of a good revision
body: Four parts of revising a draft. Select each tab to see what it asks you to do.
instruction: Select each tab to read about that part.

_items.title: Structure
_items.body: Structure is the order your points come in and how they connect. At the macro level it is the overall arrangement of the whole piece; at the micro level it is how each paragraph opens and links to the next. A reader should always be able to see what a paragraph is about and how it follows on.

_items.title: Clarity
_items.body: Clarity is writing a reader understands first time. A reliable move is the subject-verb-object sentence: say who did what to what, in that order. Using the active voice ('the owner locked the door') rather than the passive ('the door was locked') usually gives a sentence more impact and leaves less to guess.

_items.title: Editing
_items.body: Editing is where the real improvement happens. It means deleting text, adding it, changing how you express things, and creating new paragraphs. It works on the substance and shape of the writing, not just its surface, and it is worth far more than a quick read-through.

_items.title: Proofreading
_items.body: Proofreading comes last. It is polishing the text: eliminating typos and the superficial errors that are easy to correct once the writing itself is settled. It is not the same as editing, and doing only this is why many drafts still read poorly.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body:
Two students have each finished a first draft and have an hour left before the deadline.

{{learner-a}} reads the draft through once, fixes a few spelling mistakes, and submits it. The typos are gone, but the points are still in a confusing order and several sentences are hard to follow on first reading. {{learner-a}} has proofread, but not edited, polishing the surface while leaving the real problems in place.

{{learner-b}} edits first: moving one paragraph so the argument builds in order, splitting a long tangled sentence into two clear subject-verb-object sentences, and cutting a repeated point. Only then does {{learner-b}} proofread for typos. The draft now reads clearly and leads the reader through. This is getting the basics right.

Both students spent their hour. Only {{learner-b}} edited for structure and clarity before proofreading, which is what actually improved the writing.

title: Revising a draft
displayTitle: How to do it
body: These moves turn a rough draft into writing that reads well. Try them on your next draft.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Have I edited before proofreading, sorting structure and clarity before chasing typos?
Does each paragraph make one clear point and connect to the ones around it?
Are my points in an order a reader can follow?
Have I rewritten tangled sentences in subject-verb-object order so it is clear who did what?
Have I cut repetition and anything that does not answer the question?
Have I left proofreading for typos and slips until the writing itself is settled?

title: Formative check: what editing does
displayTitle: Which of these is the best description of what editing does to improve a draft?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does editing do to improve a draft?

_items.text: Reorders points, cuts or adds text, and sharpens how things are expressed.
_items.feedback: Yes. Editing works on structure and expression, the substance of the writing.

_items.text: Corrects typos and small slips once the writing is settled.
_items.feedback: That is proofreading, not editing.

_items.text: Counts the words to check the draft is long enough.
_items.feedback: Counting words is not editing.

_items.text: Reads the draft aloud without changing anything.
_items.feedback: Reading without changing anything does not improve the draft.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Editing reorders, cuts, adds and sharpens: it improves the substance of the writing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option changes the structure and expression, not just the surface?
_incorrect.final: Editing reorders points, cuts or adds text, and sharpens expression. Fixing typos is proofreading; counting words or reading without changing anything are neither.

title: Formative check: editing versus proofreading
displayTitle: In the worked example, what made the second student's revision more effective than the first's?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What made the second student's revision more effective?

_items.text: They spent longer checking their spelling.
_items.feedback: Spelling is proofreading; it is not what improved the writing most.

_items.text: They edited for structure and clarity first, and only then proofread for typos.
_items.feedback: Yes. Editing before proofreading is what made the revision effective.

_items.text: They only fixed surface errors and left the structure as it was.
_items.feedback: That is the first student's approach, which left the real problems in place.

_items.text: They submitted the draft without reading it again.
_items.feedback: They revised carefully, not carelessly.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The second student edited for structure and clarity before proofreading.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the student who sorted the bigger problems before the typos.
_incorrect.final: The second student edited for structure and clarity, then proofread. Extra spell-checking, surface-only fixes, or not revising at all are not it.

title: Formative check: matching the move
displayTitle: You are revising a draft in {{context}} whose points are in a confusing order. Which revision move fixes that problem?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which revision move fixes a confusing order of points?

_items.text: Editing: reorder the paragraphs so the points build in a sequence a reader can follow.
_items.feedback: Yes. A confusing order is a structure problem, fixed by editing, in {{context}} as anywhere.

_items.text: Proofreading: correct the typos and spelling slips.
_items.feedback: Proofreading fixes surface errors, not the order of points.

_items.text: Adding more words until the draft reaches the word count.
_items.feedback: More words do not fix a confusing order.

_items.text: Reading the draft aloud once and submitting it.
_items.feedback: Reading aloud without reordering leaves the structure problem in place.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A confusing order is a structure problem you fix by editing, reordering the paragraphs.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. A confusing order is about structure; which move changes structure?
_incorrect.final: Reordering the paragraphs by editing fixes a confusing order. Proofreading, padding the word count, or just reading aloud do not.

body: Which of these best describes academic writing, as this course presents it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Which best describes academic writing as this course presents it?

_items.text: A process of distinct stages: understanding, planning, drafting and revising.
_items.feedback: Yes. Writing is a staged process.

_items.text: A single talent that some students have and others lack.
_items.feedback: Writing is a process anyone can follow, not an inborn talent.

_items.text: One careful sitting that produces the finished piece.
_items.feedback: Writing is built in stages, not one sitting.

_items.text: A matter of writing as many words as you can.
_items.feedback: Quantity is not what makes writing good.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Academic writing is a process of distinct stages.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about the stages a piece of writing moves through.

body: A student opens a blank document and tries to write the finished essay perfectly from the first line. What is the main problem with this approach?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main problem with trying to write the finished essay perfectly from the first line?

_items.text: It collapses the whole writing process into one sitting, instead of drafting then revising.
_items.feedback: Yes. It skips the stages that make writing manageable.

_items.text: It uses too many sources.
_items.feedback: The problem is not the number of sources.

_items.text: It spends too long on planning.
_items.feedback: The problem is too little process, not too much planning.

_items.text: It proofreads before editing.
_items.feedback: The problem here is trying to be perfect first time, not the order of revision.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The problem is collapsing the process into one perfect sitting.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What stage is being skipped when you try to be perfect first time?

body: In an assignment task, what does the 'steer' refer to?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does the steer of a task refer to?

_items.text: The instruction word, such as analyse or discuss, that tells you how to approach the question.
_items.feedback: Yes. The steer sets the approach.

_items.text: The keywords that fix the topic.
_items.feedback: Those are the keywords, not the steer.

_items.text: The word count.
_items.feedback: The word count is not the steer.

_items.text: The deadline.
_items.feedback: The deadline is not the steer.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The steer is the instruction word that sets the approach.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which part tells you HOW to answer?

body: What is the main purpose of a first draft?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the main purpose of a first draft?

_items.text: To get a complete rough version down that you can then improve.
_items.feedback: Yes. A draft is raw material to improve.

_items.text: To produce finished, polished prose in one go.
_items.feedback: A first draft is meant to be rough, not finished.

_items.text: To reach the word count as quickly as possible.
_items.feedback: Hitting a word count is not the purpose of a draft.

_items.text: To avoid having to plan the essay.
_items.feedback: A draft follows a plan; it does not replace one.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A first draft gets a rough version down that you then improve.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. What is a draft for, if not to be perfect?

body: What is the difference between editing and proofreading?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What is the difference between editing and proofreading?

_items.text: Editing improves structure and expression; proofreading polishes the surface and catches typos.
_items.feedback: Yes. Editing is the bigger job; proofreading is the final polish.

_items.text: Editing fixes typos; proofreading reorders the argument.
_items.feedback: That has the two the wrong way round.

_items.text: They are two words for the same task.
_items.feedback: They are different jobs in revision.

_items.text: Editing is done by a tutor; proofreading is done by the student.
_items.feedback: Both are done by the writer.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Editing improves structure and expression; proofreading polishes the surface.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which job is about the substance, and which about the surface?

body: A reliable way to make a sentence clearer is to...
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A reliable way to make a sentence clearer is to...

_items.text: put it in subject-verb-object order, so it is clear who did what.
_items.feedback: Yes. Subject-verb-object order is a reliable clarity move.

_items.text: make it as long and detailed as possible.
_items.feedback: Length usually makes a sentence harder, not clearer.

_items.text: write it in the passive voice to sound formal.
_items.feedback: The passive often leaves more to guess; the active is usually clearer.

_items.text: add more adjectives to each noun.
_items.feedback: More adjectives do not make a sentence clearer.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Subject-verb-object order makes it clear who did what.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Which option makes a sentence easier to understand first time?

title: Orientation
body: You have now looked at three things: that writing is a process of distinct stages, how to understand a task and get a first draft down, and how to improve a draft by getting the basics right. On their own they are three separate ideas. This lesson brings them together into one process you can keep using.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are not expected to write like an expert. The aim is to see these stages as one process you work through each time, rather than three separate ideas, so the habit carries on past this course and into the rest of your studies.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

_items.text: recognise how writing as a process, planning and drafting, and revising for the basics connect as one practice
show the whole writing process at work in a worked example of a student's approach to a piece
plan how you will work through the whole writing process on your next piece of {{context}} writing

title: Concept: definition
body: Writing is one process you work through, not three separate skills. You understand the task and plan, you get a rough draft down, and then you improve that draft by getting the basics right. The three ideas from the earlier lessons are the stages of that one process, and you run them in order each time you write.

title: Concept: in practice
body: In practice, this means running the same process on every piece you write, in any subject. You read the task and plan, you get a rough draft down, and then you improve it, in that order. The piece that went through the whole process almost always beats the one written in a single sitting. Over a term, making this your normal way of working is what steadily raises the standard of your writing.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think about the next piece of writing you have coming up. How will you work through the whole process on it, from reading the task to proofreading, and where will you start?
instruction: Write a few sentences for yourself. This is not marked, and the questions have no right answers.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Academic writing is most useful when you treat it as one process, not three separate skills. You run the same stages in order every time: understand the task, plan, draft, then revise for the basics. It is making this your normal way of working, piece after piece, that steadily improves your writing.

displayTitle: Lesson Sources

See pages 93 to 94 of Chapter 6 of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: The steps as one process
displayTitle: The steps as one process
body: Writing is one process you work through each time, not three separate skills. Select each step to see what it involves.
instruction: Select each step.

_items.title: Plan
_items.body: Read the task closely, work out its steer and keywords, and make a rough plan.

_items.title: Draft
_items.body: Write a quick first draft from your plan, without worrying yet about how it sounds.

_items.title: Edit
_items.body: Edit the draft for structure and clarity, reordering points and sharpening sentences.

_items.title: Proofread
_items.body: Proofread for typos and small errors, then hand the finished piece in.

title: Worked example
displayTitle: Worked example
body: Two students are each set the same piece to write. Student A writes it in one sitting, straight to the finished version, and hands it in without planning or revising. Student B works through the whole process instead: reading the task and planning, getting a rough draft down, then editing for structure and clarity before proofreading. Both spent the same time, but Student B's piece is clearer and better organised, because it went through every stage.

title: Working with the cycle
displayTitle: How to work through the whole process
body: Use these to check you have worked through the whole process, not just part of it.
instruction: Tick each item when you have done it.

_items.text: Did I read the task for its steer and keywords before writing?
Did I make a rough plan rather than start straight into the finished piece?
Did I get a first draft down instead of waiting for perfect sentences?
Did I edit for structure and clarity before proofreading?
Will I use this same process on my next piece of writing?

displayTitle: Why is it more useful to treat writing as one process rather than three separate skills?
body: Why is it more useful to treat writing as one process rather than three separate skills?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Why is it more useful to treat writing as one process rather than three separate skills?

_items.text: Because each stage feeds the next: understanding the task shapes your plan, your plan shapes your draft, and your draft is what you then improve.
_items.feedback: Yes. The stages connect, so working through them in order makes each one easier.

_items.text: Because working through one stage well means you can skip the others.
_items.feedback: No. The point is that the stages connect, not that any one replaces the rest.

_items.text: Because it means you never have to plan or revise.
_items.feedback: Not so. Planning and revising are stages of the one process, not things it removes.

_items.text: Because one process takes less thought than learning three skills.
_items.feedback: The gain is not less thought. It is that the stages feed one another.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Writing is one process whose stages feed one another, worked through in order.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about how each stage sets up the next one.

displayTitle: A student reads a task closely and plans, writes a rough first draft, then edits it for structure and clarity before proofreading. What does this show?
body: A student reads a task closely and plans, writes a rough first draft, then edits it for structure and clarity before proofreading. What does this show?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: A student reads a task closely and plans, writes a rough first draft, then edits it for structure and clarity before proofreading. What does this show?

_items.text: That the student is using the whole writing process: each stage leads into the next, from task to finished piece.
_items.feedback: Yes. Every stage is there, in order, working as one process.

_items.text: That the student is wasting time by doing more than one piece of writing needs.
_items.feedback: No. Each stage does a different job, and together they make the piece stronger.

_items.text: That only the proofreading at the end really matters.
_items.feedback: Not so. The earlier stages did the real work, and proofreading only polishes the surface.

_items.text: That planning and editing are the same stage.
_items.feedback: They are different stages: planning comes before the draft, and editing improves it afterwards.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The student worked through the whole process, each stage feeding the next.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Notice how the student moves through every stage in order.

displayTitle: You want to use this whole process to improve your {{context}} writing this term. Which plan best treats writing as one process you work through?
body: You want to use this whole process to improve your {{context}} writing this term. Which plan best treats writing as one process you work through?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: You want to use this whole process to improve your your subject writing this term. Which plan best treats writing as one process you work through?

_items.text: On each piece, read the task and plan, get a rough draft down, then edit for structure and clarity before proofreading.
_items.feedback: Yes. That works through every stage, in order, each time you write.

_items.text: Write each piece in one careful sitting and hand it in without revising.
_items.feedback: That drops the drafting and revising stages, which is where most of the work happens.

_items.text: Only plan the pieces you find hard, and skip planning on the rest.
_items.feedback: Planning is part of the one process you use every time, not only when a task feels hard.

_items.text: Proofread everything twice and leave the structure as it is.
_items.feedback: Proofreading is the last stage, and it cannot fix a structure you never edited.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The whole process, worked through in order, is what you use on every piece.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Look for the plan that works through every stage, not just one.
